subject: body
title: Eyes and Ears
about: How seeing and hearing work, not which sense is which: the pupil that lets light in and grows in the dark, the lens that focuses, the brain that makes the picture, two eyes for judging distance, eyelids, lashes, tears and glasses; then the outer ear that catches sound, the eardrum that vibrates, the three tiny bones, the snail-shaped inner ear, two ears for finding where a sound comes from, earwax, balance, and keeping loud sounds down. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.PCH.2.1 (avoiding injury: loud sounds, poking ears) and 1.ICHR.1.2 (what makes each person special: glasses, and eyes and ears that work differently). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he watches his pupils change in a mirror.
tip: Dim the lights and watch his pupils grow in a mirror, then flick the light on and watch them shrink.

cards.q: Look in a mirror. What is the black circle in the middle of your eye?
cards.note: The pupil is really a hole. Light goes through it into your eye.

cards.q: You walk into a dark room. What does your pupil do?
cards.note: A bigger pupil lets in more light so you can see in the dark. In bright sun it shrinks to a dot.

cards.q: Behind the pupil is a clear lens. What does it do with the light?
cards.note: The lens bends light to make a sharp picture at the back of your eye, like a camera.

cards.q: The back of your eye catches the light. Who turns it into the picture you see?
cards.note: The eye sends a message along a nerve. The brain makes the picture, even flipping it right side up.

cards.q: Why is seeing with two eyes better than with one?
cards.note: Each eye sees a slightly different view, and the brain uses both to judge distance. Try catching a ball with one eye shut!

cards.q: What closes over your eyes when you blink or sleep?
cards.note: Blinking spreads tears over your eyes to keep them wet and clean, about 15 times every minute.

cards.q: What are the tiny hairs along the edge of your eyelids for?
cards.note: Eyelashes catch dust and tell your eyelid to blink when something comes too close.

cards.q: You cry a little and your nose gets runny too. Where do the extra teardrops go?
cards.note: A tiny tube in the corner of each eye drains tears into the nose. That is why crying makes your nose run.

cards.q: Glasses help blurry eyes see sharp. How do they do it?
cards.note: Glasses bend light a little before it reaches the eye, so the picture lands sharp. Many kids and grown-ups wear them.

cards.q: The part of your ear you can see is shaped like a cup. What is it for?
cards.note: Cup your hands behind your ears and listen. Bigger cups catch more sound.

cards.q: Sound goes into your ear and hits a thin skin stretched tight like a drum. What is it?
cards.note: Sound makes the eardrum shake, or vibrate, like a drum top when you tap it.

cards.q: Behind the eardrum sit three tiny bones. What do they do with the shaking?
cards.note: They are the smallest bones you have, called the hammer, anvil and stirrup.

cards.q: Deep in your ear is a part curled like a snail shell. What does it do?
cards.note: It is called the cochlea, say KOK-lee-uh. Tiny hairs inside it send sound messages along a nerve to the brain.

cards.q: Two ears are better than one for knowing...?
cards.note: A sound reaches one ear a tiny bit sooner and louder. The brain uses that to point you the right way.

cards.q: A sound is so loud it hurts your ears. What should you do?
cards.note: Very loud sounds can hurt the tiny hairs inside the ear, and they do not grow back. Keep headphones low.

cards.q: The sticky yellow stuff inside your ear is earwax. What is it for?
cards.note: Earwax protects the ear and slowly moves out on its own. Never poke anything inside your ear.

cards.q: You spin around and feel dizzy. Which part of you helps keep your balance?
cards.note: Tiny loops of liquid in the inner ear tell the brain which way is up. Spinning sloshes them, so you feel dizzy for a moment.
